summary: You produced a correct brute-force pair search that passes most tests, but it fails the edge-case contract used by this harness (empty input expects [] rather than an exception). You also correctly identified the optimal hash-map approach, but didn’t implement it, leaving the solution at O(n^2) which is not aligned with the expected performance under the stated constraints.

test_results.summary_note: Passed core cases; failed the empty-input edge case due to raising ValueError instead of returning [].

thinking_and_logic: Your approach was a straightforward nested-loop search over all index pairs (i, j) with j > i, returning as soon as a matching sum is found. This guarantees finding the unique solution when it exists, but it assumes the input always satisfies the constraints; the test harness included an empty-input edge case that violated that assumption, and the code raised instead of returning an empty result.
code_assessment: The final code matches the brute-force approach from the answer key (O(n^2) time, O(1) space). Compared to the canonical optimal solution (single pass + hash map of seen value->index, check complement before insert), your code does not scale to the upper constraint (1e5) in principle and it also diverges from expected behavior on empty/no-solution inputs by throwing an exception rather than returning []. The optimal hash-map approach achieves O(n) time and is the expected default for this problem under these constraints.

next_steps.action: Implement the single-pass hash map Two Sum pattern (seen[value] = index; if target-value in seen, return [seen[comp], i]).
next_steps.why: It reduces time from O(n^2) to O(n), which is the canonical expectation for n up to 1e5.
next_steps.how: Write it in one loop, check complement before inserting current value to avoid using the same element twice; keep return format consistent.

next_steps.action: Add an explicit output-contract guard for empty/no-solution cases (return []).
next_steps.why: Your only recorded failure was returning via exception rather than the expected sentinel value.
next_steps.how: At the top: if not nums: return []; and at the end: return [] instead of raising (unless the prompt explicitly requires an error).

next_steps.action: Practice “sorted array” Two Sum with two pointers.
next_steps.why: It’s a common follow-up that tests whether you can switch patterns based on input properties (O(n) time, O(1) space).
next_steps.how: Use l/r pointers; move l if sum<target else move r; return indices accordingly (or values depending on prompt).

encouragement: You’re close: you had a correct baseline and you already knew the optimal approach—focus on shipping the hash-map version and doing a quick edge-case contract check before submitting.

Let me restate: I need two distinct indices whose values sum to the target. I'll start with the straightforward approach — check every pair with two loops — and optimize if there's time.
Writing the nested loops now. Outer loop i, inner loop from i plus one so I don't reuse the same element.
Okay, it works on the example. Running the visible tests.
Before you finish — consider whether there are any unusual inputs worth checking.
Unusual inputs... duplicates should be fine since I use indices. I think I'm good, submitting.
One of the visible tests failed — the empty input case. You raised an error instead of returning an empty list.
Ah, I see. I assumed there's always a solution because of the constraints, so I raised. I'd need a guard for empty or no-solution inputs.
What's the complexity of your solution?
Two nested loops, so O(n squared) time and constant space. I know a hash map would make it O(n) but I didn't get to it.
